articles.title: How Revolutionary, Really, Was Christianity?
articles.author: Molly Judd
articles.content_excerpt: In the Acts of the Apostles, the followers of Jesus Christ are repeatedly described as belonging to “the Way.” In the modern Christian lexicon, this phrase is often understood as a spiritual path rather than a physical one. One travels the Way from a life without Christ to one with him. Returning to the original ancient Greek texts, the classicist Tim Whitmarsh points out that the word that underpins the idea of the Way, hodos , can mean a spiritual path, but it can also, and more often, means a physical road — or a journey along one. Paul and other early Christian missionaries were on a spiritual journey, but they were also on what Whitmarsh calls a literal road trip, traveling across modern-day Turkey, Syria, Greece, and elsewhere to convert anyone who would listen. It was 2020, and Matt DeBoth and Angel Escobar were canvassing Koreatown, Highland Park and other gentrifying Los Angeles neighborhoods, trying to get tenants, mostly working-class immigrants, to give up some of the city’s most affordable apartments. Each time a tenant agreed, DeBoth later said in a deposition, he and Escobar could get a bonus of up to $1,000. They worked for K3 Holdings LLC, a landlord based in Beverly Hills, California, which was rapidly acquiring dozens of rent-controlled properties across L.A. articles.content_excerpt: Silkwood , a 1983 dramatization of the life of worker-activist Karen Silkwood , starring Cher, Kurt Russell and Meryl Streep, is the best and probably the only Hollywood movie about occupational safety and health. It tells the story of the transformation of Silkwood from a carefree worker in a Kerr-McGee nuclear processing plant into a soberly effective opponent of corporate malfeasance. The focus is on her, but the changing attitudes of her coworkers play an important supporting role. articles.title: Chattel Slavery vs. Wage Labor: Who Is Really Free?
articles.author: Sharon Kyle
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In 1860, nearly four million Black people were enslaved in the United States. Their labor produced enormous wealth, but they had virtually no control over what they made or who benefited from it. They planted and harvested cotton, cultivated tobacco and sugar, built homes, maintained households, and practiced skilled trades. Today, American workers produce goods and services on a scale unimaginable in 1860. Yet millions struggle to afford housing, healthcare, education, childcare, food, and retirement. Memory loss changes how a person moves through the day, manages medication, and responds to unfamiliar situations.
